label: Abel the righteous shepherd
def: Adam's younger son, a keeper of sheep whose offering God accepted, killed in the field by his envious elder brother Cain; his blood cried out to God from the ground.
christ: Christ is the righteous shepherd slain by His own brethren, and His blood "speaketh better things than that of Abel" (Heb 12:24): it "has cleansed all men, and sends forth a voice more clear and more distinct" (Chrysostom, *Hom. Heb.* 32). What was "acted beforehand in Abel" was "accomplished in the Lord's person" (Irenaeus, *AH* 4.34.4).
where: Irenaeus, *AH* 4.34.4 — “These things were acted beforehand in Abel, were also previously declared by the prophets, but were accomplished in the Lord's person”
Clement of Alexandria, *Paed.* 1.6 — “for the righteous man of old is the type of the new righteous one; and the blood of old that interceded, intercedes in the place of the new blood.”
Cyprian, *Pat.* 10 — “Thus Abel, who first initiated and consecrated the origin of martyrdom, and the passion of the righteous man”
Augustine, *C. Faust.* 12.9 — “Abel, the younger brother, is killed by the elder brother; Christ, the head of the younger people, is killed by the elder people of the Jews.”
Augustine, *City of God* 15.7 — “He was also a figure of the Jews who slew Christ the Shepherd of the flock of men, prefigured by Abel the shepherd of sheep”
Chrysostom, *Hom. Heb.* 32 — “For this has cleansed all men, and sends forth a voice more clear and more distinct, in proportion as it has greater testimony, namely that by facts.”

label: Above and below
def: What is above gives its quality to what is below; earthly signs come first and carry heavenly effects.
christ: The heavenly things belong to Christ, not to John, who only prepares for them: John "professes that the celestial things are not his, but Christ's" (Tertullian, *Bapt.* 10).
where: Tertullian, *Bapt.* 4 — “an underlying material substance should catch the quality of that which overhangs it”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 3 — “the material substance which governs terrestrial life acts as agent likewise in the celestial.”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 10 — “John himself professes that the celestial things are not his, but Christ's”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 1.4.12 — “he who passes through this font, that is from earthly to heavenly things”
Origen, *DP* 4.1.13 (Gk.) — “of what heavenly things the Jews "according to the flesh" served as an example and a shadow”

label: Adam and the second Adam
def: The first man, whose disobedience brought death, and Christ, the second, who replays and reverses his story.
christ: Christ is the second Adam, made from virgin "earth" (Mary) to keep the analogy (Irenaeus, *AH* 3.21.10).
where: Irenaeus, *AH* 3.18.7 — “as by the disobedience of the one man who was originally moulded from virgin soil, the many were made sinners”
Irenaeus, *AH* 3.21.10 — “recapitulating Adam in Himself, rightly receive a birth, enabling Him to gather up Adam [into Himself], from Mary, who was as yet a virgin.”
Irenaeus, *AH* 3.22.3 — “Hence also was Adam himself termed by Paul "the figure of Him that was to come,"”
Irenaeus, *AH* 5.16.3 — “In the second Adam, however, we are reconciled, being made obedient even unto death.”
Irenaeus, *AH* 5.21.1 — “as our species went down to death through a vanquished man, so we may ascend to life again through a victorious one”
Cyril, *Cat.* 13.31 — “Very speedily I passed sentence upon Adam, very speedily I pardon thee.”
Cyril, *Myst.* 2.2 — “ye bore the likeness of the first-formed Adam, who was naked in the garden, and was not ashamed.”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 5.3.14 — “Thou becamest a dry tree in Adam; but now through the grace of Christ thou hast budded into a fruitful tree.”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶12 — “No longer shall Adam be confounded when called by Thee, nor hide himself”

label: Ark / ship (vessel through the waters)
def: A closed wooden vessel that carries the righteous through the drowning waters; read as the Church, and its wood as the cross.
christ: The ark is the Church (Tertullian, Cyril), its wood is the cross (Ambrose), and Christ is "the true Noe" (Cyril, *Cat.* 17.10). In the boat Christ sleeps and then calms the world (Tertullian, *Bapt.* 12).
where: Tertullian, *Bapt.* 8 — “sent out from the heavens where is the Church, the typified ark.”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 12 — “that little ship did present a figure of the Church, in that she is disquieted "in the sea," that is, in the world”
Cyril, *Procat.* 14 — “For now I need the example of Noah's ark” ... “If the Church is shut, and you are all inside”
Cyril, *Cat.* 13.20 — “in the time of Noe the preservation of life was by an ark of wood.”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 3.10 — “You see the water, you see the wood [of the ark], you see the dove”
Cyril, *Cat.* 17.10 — “of whom the various dispositions of the animals in the ark were a figure”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶8 — “laid in an ark, for it was fitting that the Law should typically be enclosed in a coffer”

label: Ark of the covenant
def: The chest of incorruptible wood overlaid with gold within and without, holding the tablets of the Law, the jar of manna and Aaron's rod, beneath the cherubim of the mercy seat.
christ: Christ's sinless flesh, made of incorruptible wood and clothed in the gold of His Godhead: "an ark of incorruptible wood was the Saviour Himself" (Hippolytus, *On Ps. 23*, in Theodoret, *Eranistes* I). Augustine notes that some have understood "the Body of Christ, that was born of Mary" to be the ark (*En. Ps.* 132 (Lat. 131).8). Hippolytus also reads it of the Virgin who bore Him, "with the Word within and the Holy Spirit without" (*On Daniel* 2.6), as does a homily once credited to Gregory Thaumaturgus.
where: Irenaeus (attributed), *Fragments* 48 — “so is that ark declared a type of the body of Christ, which is both pure and immaculate”
Hippolytus, *On Daniel* 2.6 — “(born) of the Virgin, who was the "ark overlaid with pure gold," with the Word within and the Holy Spirit without”
Hippolytus, *On Ps. 23* (in Theodoret, *Eranistes* I) — “And an ark of incorruptible wood was the Saviour Himself”
Ps.-Gregory Thaumaturgus, *Hom. 1 on the Annunciation* — “For the holy Virgin is in truth an ark, wrought with gold both within and without, that has received the whole treasury of the sanctuary.”
Augustine, *En. Ps.* 132 (Lat. 131).8 — “The Body of Christ, that was born of Mary, hath been understood by some to be the ark of sanctification”

links.label: Hippolytus, On Ps. 23 (in Theodoret, Eranistes I)
Ps.-Gregory Thaumaturgus, Hom. 1 on the Annunciation

label: Baptismal font (grave and mother)
def: The water of baptism, which is at once a tomb to go down into and a womb to be born from.
christ: Going into the font is going into Christ's tomb (Cyril, *Myst.* 2.4).
where: Cyril, *Myst.* 2.4 — “that Water of salvation was at once your grave and your mother.”
Cyril, *Myst.* 2.4 — “ye were led to the holy pool of Divine Baptism, as Christ was carried from the Cross to the Sepulchre”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 2.6.19 — “the font is, as it were, a burial”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 4.23 — “that pool was as a type, that you might believe that the power of God descends upon this font.”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 1 — “we, little fishes, after the example of our IChThUS Jesus Christ, are born in water”

label: Bread from heaven
def: Food rained from heaven in the wilderness; a shadow of the living bread that does not die.
christ: Christ's Body is the living bread (Ambrose, *De Myst.* 8.47).
where: Ambrose, *De Myst.* 8.47 — “But yet all those who ate that food died in the wilderness”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 8.49a — “That manna came from heaven, this is above the heavens”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 8.49b — “light is better than shadow, truth than a figure, the Body of its Giver than the manna from heaven.”
Cyril, *Myst.* 4.5 — “in the New Testament there is Bread of heaven, and a Cup of salvation”

label: Christ's opened side (water and blood)
def: The wound in Christ's side, from which water and blood flow: the two baptisms and the sacraments.
christ: The side is Christ's own. The Fathers make it the source of baptism (water) and martyrdom or the cup (blood).
where: Tertullian, *Bapt.* 9 — “when He is wounded, forth from His side bursts water; witness the soldier's lance!”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 16 — “These two baptisms He sent out from the wound in His pierced side”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.10 — “He shed forth blood and water; that men, living in times of peace, might be baptized in water”
Cyril, *Cat.* 13.20 — “from the side of Jesus the water flowed upon the wood.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 13.21 — “Jesus at the last gave forth from His side water with blood.”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 5.1.4 — “Why from his side? Because whence the guilt, thence the grace; guilt through woman, grace through the Lord Jesus Christ.”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 4.20 — “the three witnesses in baptism, the water, the blood, and the Spirit, are one”
Irenaeus, *AH* 3.22.2 — “nor, when His side was pierced, would there have come forth blood and water.”

label: Crossing the water, then testing in the wilderness
def: After passing through water comes a period of testing in the desert, numbered forty.
christ: Christ repeats Israel's forty years as forty days and wins where Israel failed. Tertullian: "the Lord figuratively retorted upon Israel the reproach".
where: Tertullian, *Bapt.* 20 — “the people, after crossing the sea, and being carried about in the desert during forty years”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 20 — “the Lord, driven apart into desert places after baptism, showed, by maintaining a fast of forty days”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.13 — “For as after His Baptism He was tempted forty days”
Cyril, *Myst.* 3.4 — “as Christ after His Baptism, and the visitation of the Holy Ghost, went forth and vanquished the adversary”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 1.4.12 — “Yet the Jews who passed through all died in the wilderness.”

label: David the shepherd king
def: The shepherd boy from Bethlehem, anointed king, who kills Goliath with a stone and is promised a son whose throne will last for ever.
christ: Christ is "our David" (Augustine, *En. Ps.* 144 (Lat. 143).1): the shepherd who becomes king, who overthrows the devil as David felled Goliath, and the Son of David whose kingdom has no end. The promise to David is fulfilled "in Christ our Lord", not in Solomon (Augustine, *City of God* 17.8).
where: Augustine, *En. Ps.* 144 (Lat. 143).1 — “This our David also did, He overthrew the devil with his own weapons”
Cyprian, *Test.* 2.16 — “with which David smote the forehead of Goliath and slew him; signifying that the devil and his servants are thereby thrown down”
Augustine, *En. Ps.* 78 (Lat. 77).37 — “This David indeed, of whose seed the flesh of Christ is, from the pastoral care of cattle was translated to the kingdom of men”
Augustine, *City of God* 17.8 — “to see the fulfillment of these things save in Christ our Lord, who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh”
Chrysostom, *Hom. Matt.* 2.6 — “both Ezekiel and other prophets besides speak of David as coming and rising again; not meaning him that was dead”
Aphrahat, *Dem.* 21.13 — “Also David was persecuted, as Jesus was persecuted. David was anointed by Samuel to be king instead of Saul who had sinned”

label: Deliverance through the sea
def: People in bondage → sign of blood → pursued to the water → pass through → enemy drowned → freedom in the wilderness.
christ: Christ is the new Moses and the Lamb. The font is the sea where Satan "disappears" (Cyril, *Myst.* 1.3).
where: Cyril, *Myst.* 1.2 — “the door posts were anointed with the blood of a lamb, that the destroyer might flee from the houses”
Cyril, *Myst.* 1.3 — “Now turn from the old to the new, from the figure to the reality.”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 9 — “What figure more manifestly fulfilled in the sacrament of baptism?”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 3.12 — “holy baptism was prefigured in that passage of the Hebrews, wherein the Egyptian perished, the Hebrew escaped.”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 1.4.12 — “he who passes through this font, dies not, but rises again.”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 1.6.20 — “to them in a figure, but to us in reality.”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶8 — “The people passed over, and the Egyptian king with his host was engulfed, and by these actions this Sacrament was foretold.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.5 — “for Israel deliverance from Pharaoh was through the sea, and for the world deliverance from sins by the washing of water with the word”

label: Dove (herald of peace; the Spirit)
def: A bird sent out or coming down after the waters, bringing peace; read as the Holy Spirit and as simplicity.
christ: The Spirit comes down on Christ at the Jordan, "the true Noe" (Cyril, *Cat.* 17.10). Through Him, the dove then comes on the baptized.
where: Tertullian, *Bapt.* 8 — “a dove was the herald which announced to the earth the assuagement of celestial wrath”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 8 — “after its old sins flies the dove of the Holy Spirit, bringing us the peace of God, sent out from the heavens”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 8 — “the dove is without literal gall”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 3.11 — “The dove is that in the form of which the Holy Spirit descended”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 4.24 — “that dove also which just Noah sent forth from the ark was a likeness of this dove”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 4.25 — “Rightly, then, did He descend like a dove, in order to admonish us that we ought to have the simplicity of the dove.”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 1.5.17 — “The Holy Spirit, however, descended from heaven, not in the reality of a dove, but in the likeness of a dove.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 17.10 — “the dove of Noe, according to some, was in part a figure”
Cyril, *Cat.* 17.9 — “He came down in the form of a dove, as some say, to exhibit a figure of that dove who is pure and innocent”
Augustine, *DDC* 2.16.24 — “perpetual peace is indicated by the olive branch which the dove brought with it when it returned to the ark”
Irenaeus, *AH* 5.19.1 — “the coming of the serpent is conquered by the harmlessness of the dove”

label: Down into the water, up into life
def: Go down into water as into a grave (three times), come up as from the tomb, newborn.
christ: This is the participation in Christ's death, burial and resurrection: in His case "there was death in reality", but in ours "only a likeness of death and sufferings, whereas of salvation there was not a likeness but a reality" (Cyril, *Myst.* 2.7).
where: Cyril, *Myst.* 2.4 — “descended three times into the water, and ascended again; here also hinting by a symbol at the three days burial of Christ.”
Cyril, *Myst.* 2.4 — “in the descent, as in the night, ye saw nothing, but in ascending again ye were as in the day.”
Cyril, *Myst.* 2.5 — “our imitation was in a figure, and our salvation in reality.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.12 — “Having gone down dead in sins, thou comest up quickened in righteousness.”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 4.21 — “you died to the world, and rose again to God.”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 2.6.19 — “a means was found that man might die while living, and while living rise again.”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 2.7.20 — “for he who is buried with Christ, rises again with Christ.”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶5 — “went beneath the fourth of these, the earth, that He might raise up life from thence.”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶5 — “coming to the element akin to earth, to water, we conceal ourselves in that as the Saviour did in the earth”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 2 — “a man is dipped in water, and amid the utterance of some few words, is sprinkled, and then rises again”

label: Dragon / whale in the waters
def: The beast in the waters (the dragon of Job, Jonah's whale) that swallows; read as the devil or death.
christ: Christ goes down into the Jordan to "break the heads of the dragon" (Cyril, *Cat.* 3.11), and into death so that death "might cast up those whom he had devoured" (Cyril, *Cat.* 14.17).
where: Cyril, *Cat.* 3.11 — “According to Job, there was in the waters the dragon that draweth up Jordan into his mouth.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.11 — “The Life encountered him, that the mouth of Death might henceforth be stopped”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.12 — “suffereth thee not afterwards to be swallowed up by the terrible dragon.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 14.17 — “where the invisible whale of death is”
Irenaeus, *AH* 3.20.1 — “did God permit man to be swallowed up by the great whale, who was the author of transgression”

label: Egypt (the house of bondage)
def: The land of bondage that the people leave through water; read spiritually as the world under sin.
christ: Christ is sent "into the world" as Moses was sent to Egypt (Cyril, *Myst.* 1.3).
where: Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶8 — “fleeing from Egypt, from the burden of sin, it is set free and saved”
Cyril, *Myst.* 1.2 — “God sent Moses to bring them out of the evil bondage of the Egyptians.”
Origen, *DP* 4.1.22 (Gk.) — “For if there be "spiritual" Israelites, it follows that there are also "spiritual" Egyptians and Babylonians.”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 9 — “The nations are set free from the world by means of water”

label: Eve and the Virgin Mary
def: Eve, still a virgin in Paradise, listens to the serpent, disobeys God and becomes the mother of all who die.
christ: Mary, a virgin who believes the angel and obeys, undoes what Eve did, so that Christ is born the same way the fall came in and destroys the serpent's work: "the knot of Eve's disobedience was loosed by the obedience of Mary" (Irenaeus, *AH* 3.22.4).
where: Justin, *Dial.* 100 — “For Eve, who was a virgin and undefiled, having conceived the word of the serpent, brought forth disobedience and death.”
Irenaeus, *AH* 3.22.4 — “For what the virgin Eve had bound fast through unbelief, this did the virgin Mary set free through faith.”
Irenaeus, *AH* 5.19.1 — “in order that the Virgin Mary might become the patroness (advocata) of the virgin Eve.”
Tertullian, *Carn.* 17 — “As Eve had believed the serpent, so Mary believed the angel.”
Jerome, *Ep.* 22.21 — “Death came through Eve, but life has come through Mary.”
Ephraim, *Hom. on Our Lord* 3 — “But Mary budded forth, a new shoot from Eve the ancient vine; and new life dwelt in her”

label: Fig leaves and the cursed fig tree
def: Fig leaves were the first covering of shame; Christ curses a fig tree with leaves but no fruit, cancelling that sign.
christ: Christ cancels the curse represented by the leaves (Cyril).
where: Cyril, *Cat.* 13.18 — “At the time of the sin, they clothed themselves with fig-leaves; for this cause Jesus also made the fig-tree the last of His signs.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 13.18 — “He curses the fig-tree, not every fig-tree, but that one alone, for the sake of the figure”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶12 — “Thou didst strip off the fig-tree leaves, an unseemly covering, and put upon us a costly garment”

label: Fire kindled on drenched wood
def: Water is poured three times on the sacrifice and fire falls from heaven and kindles it.
christ: Gregory of Nyssa reads it as faith in the Trinity and as the Spirit given in baptism. Cyril calls Christ the one “that baptizeth with the Holy Ghost and with fire” (*Cat.* 3.9).
where: Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶9 — “the fire was kindled by water thrice poured upon it”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶9 — “where the mystic water is, there is the kindling, warm, and fiery Spirit, that burns up the ungodly, and illuminates the faithful.”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 5.26 — “when Elijah prayed, fire was sent forth and consecrated the sacrifice.”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 5.27 — “To those [of old] a visible fire was sent that they might believe; for us who believe, the Lord works invisibly”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 10 — “true and stable faith is baptized with water, unto salvation; pretended and weak faith is baptized with fire, unto judgment.”

label: Forty
def: The number of fasting and testing (Moses, Elijah, Christ; Israel's years), read as life in time abstaining for eternity.
christ: Christ's forty-day fast fulfils Moses and Elijah and reverses Israel's forty years (Tertullian, *Bapt.* 20).
where: Augustine, *DDC* 2.16.25 — “Moses and Elijah, and our Lord Himself, all fasted for forty days.”
Augustine, *DDC* 2.16.25 — “the number contains ten four times, indicating the knowledge of all things, and that knowledge interwoven with time.”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 20 — “the people, after crossing the sea, and being carried about in the desert during forty years”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 20 — “by maintaining a fast of forty days, that the man of God lives "not by bread alone,"”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.13 — “For as after His Baptism He was tempted forty days”
Irenaeus, *AH* 5.21.2 — “Fasting forty days, like Moses and Elias, He afterwards hungered”
Irenaeus, *AH* 3.22.2 — “fasting those forty days, like Moses and Elias”

label: Gideon's fleece, wet then dry
def: A woollen fleece that Gideon laid on the threshing-floor: first the dew fell on the fleece alone while the ground stayed dry, then on the ground alone while the fleece stayed dry.
christ: Irenaeus, Ambrose and Augustine read the dew as Christ and the grace of His Spirit, given first to Israel alone and then poured over all the nations while Israel is left dry; Cyril reads the rain falling silently into the fleece as the Word coming down into flesh: "rain, because of His heavenly nature, and into a fleece, because of His humanity" (Cyril, *Cat.* 12.9).
where: Irenaeus, *AH* 3.17.3 — “prophesied that there would be dryness upon the fleece of wool (a type of the people), on which alone at first there had been dew”
Ambrose, *De Spir. S.* 1 prol. 7 — “the dew of moistening faith dried up in the breasts of the Jews, and that divine Fountain turned away its course to the hearts of the Gentiles.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 12.9 — “rain, because of His heavenly nature, and into a fleece, because of His humanity.”
Augustine, *En. Ps.* 72 (Lat. 71).9 — “The same Christ therefore Himself came down like rain upon a fleece, when yet the floor was dry”
Augustine, *C. Faust.* 12.32 — “the Hebrew nation at first possessing alone in its typical institution Christ the mystery of God, while the whole world was in ignorance?”

label: Going down, coming up
def: The vertical movement of going down (water, earth, Hades) and coming back up (life, heaven), by Christ and in baptism.
christ: Christ goes down first (into the Jordan, into Hades) and brings others up with Him.
where: Cyril, *Cat.* 3.12 — “Having gone down dead in sins, thou comest up quickened in righteousness.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 14.18 — “who descended into hell alone, but ascended thence with a great company”
Cyril, *Myst.* 2.4 — “descended three times into the water, and ascended again”
Irenaeus, *AH* 5.21.1 — “as our species went down to death through a vanquished man, so we may ascend to life again through a victorious one”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.5 — “for first he crosses the Jordan, then in a chariot mounts the heaven.”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶5 — “that He might bring the Spirit from above, and exalt man to heaven”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 1.5.18 — “But Christ descended first, the Spirit followed.”

label: Isaac offered on Moriah
def: Abraham's only son, whom God told him to offer on a mountain in Moriah; Isaac carried the wood up himself, was spared at the last moment, and a ram caught in a thicket was offered in his place.
christ: The Father giving up His only Son, who carried the wood of His own cross; the ram caught by the horns is Christ crowned with thorns and offered in our place, and Isaac coming back alive points to the resurrection. Isaac "carried to the place of sacrifice the wood on which he was to be offered up, just as the Lord Himself carried His own cross" (Augustine, *City of God* 16.32).
where: Tertullian, *Adv. Marc.* 3.18 — “First, then, Isaac, when he was given up by his father as an offering, himself carried the wood for his own death.”
Irenaeus, *AH* 4.5.4 — “in order that God also might be pleased to offer up for all his seed His own beloved and only-begotten Son, as a sacrifice for our redemption.”
Clement of Alexandria, *Paed.* 1.5 — “Isaac only bore the wood of the sacrifice, as the Lord the wood of the cross.”
Cyprian, *Pat.* 10 — “And Isaac, prefigured as the likeness of the Lord's victim, when he is presented by his father for immolation, is found patient.”
Augustine, *C. Faust.* 12.25 — “Who in Isaac carried the wood for His own sacrifice, but He who carried His own cross?”
Augustine, *City of God* 16.32 — “What, then, did he represent but Jesus, who, before He was offered up, was crowned with thorns by the Jews?”

label: Jacob's ladder and anointed stone
def: The ladder Jacob saw in a dream at Bethel, set on the earth and reaching to heaven with angels going up and down on it, and the stone under his head which he then set up and anointed with oil.
christ: Christ is the ladder joining earth to heaven and the gate by which heaven is entered, on whom the angels ascend and descend as He said to Nathanael; the stone Jacob anointed is Christ, the Anointed One. "Christ is the ladder reaching from earth to heaven" (Augustine, *C. Faust.* 12.26).
where: Justin, *Dial.* 86 — “that the stone symbolically proclaimed Christ, we have also proved by many Scriptures”
Tertullian, *Adv. Marc.* 3.24 — “For he had seen Christ the Lord, the temple of God, and also the gate by whom heaven is entered.”
Cyprian, *Test.* 2.16 — “This is the stone in Genesis, which Jacob places at his head, because the head of the man is Christ”
Augustine, *C. Faust.* 12.26 — “Christ is the ladder reaching from earth to heaven, or from the carnal to the spiritual”
Augustine, *En. Ps.* 45 (Lat. 44).18 — “In that "stone" he understood Christ; for that reason he anointed it.”

label: Jerusalem above
def: The heavenly city that is the true subject of what is said about Jerusalem, Judea and Israel.
christ: The Fathers do not tie it to Christ directly. It is the goal of the people Christ leads.
where: Origen, *DP* 4.1.22 (Gk.) — “it follows that the cities of Israel have for their metropolis the heavenly Jerusalem”
Origen, *DP* 4.1.22 (Gk.) — “we must understand the Scriptures as speaking of the heavenly city”
Augustine, *DDC* 3.34.47 — “such as Tyre or Babylon, are things said in Scripture whose significance oversteps the limits of the city”

label: Joseph sold by his brothers
def: Jacob's beloved son, hated by his brothers, thrown into a pit and sold into Egypt, who rose from prison to rule over Egypt and fed the brothers who had sold him.
christ: Christ, hated and sold by His own brethren, who after His sufferings is exalted and gives bread to the nations, forgiving those who betrayed Him. "Christ appears to me in Joseph, who was persecuted and sold by his brethren, and after his troubles obtained honor in Egypt" (Augustine, *C. Faust.* 12.28).
where: Tertullian, *Adv. Jud.* 10 — “he suffered persecution at the hands of his brethren, and was sold into Egypt, on account of the favour of God; just as Christ was sold by Israel”
Cyprian, *Pat.* 10 — “Joseph, sold by his brethren and sent away, not only with patience pardons them, but even bountifully and mercifully bestows gratuitous supplies of corn on them”
Ambrose, *De Spir. S.* 3.17.124 — “For both in the patriarch Joseph was there a type of Christ, and Christ Himself came in the truth of His Body”
Chrysostom, *Hom. Acts* 16 — “Though they had no fault to find with him, and though he came on purpose to bring them their food, they thus ill-treated him.”
Augustine, *C. Faust.* 12.28 — “Christ appears to me in Joseph, who was persecuted and sold by his brethren, and after his troubles obtained honor in Egypt.”
Augustine, *En. Ps.* 81 (Lat. 80).8 — “There Joseph after tribulations was exalted, and here Christ, after the suffering of the Martyrs, was glorified.”

label: Joshua (Jesus son of Nun)
def: Moses' successor, renamed Joshua (in Greek, Jesus), who leads the people across the Jordan into the promised land that Moses could not enter, and divides it among them.
christ: Joshua bears the Lord's own name and does what Moses (the Law) could not: Jesus brings His people into the true land of promise, eternal life. He was "in many things a type of Him" (Cyril, *Cat.* 10.11), "ordained as a type of this mystery" (Tertullian, *Adv. Marc.* 3.16).
where: Justin, *Dial.* 113 — “the former gave them a temporary inheritance, seeing he was neither Christ who is God, nor the Son of God; but the latter, after the holy resurrection, shall give us the eternal possession”
Tertullian, *Adv. Marc.* 3.16 — “that great man, who was ordained as a type of this mystery, was actually consecrated with the figure of the Lord's own name, being called Joshua.”
Barnabas, *Ep.* 12 — “Behold again: Jesus who was manifested, both by type and in the flesh, is not the Son of man, but the Son of God.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 10.11 — “And Jesus the son of Nave was in many things a type of Him. For when he began to rule over the people, he began from Jordan”
Augustine, *City of God* 16.43 — “not Moses, who received the law for the people on Mount Sinai, that led the people into the land of promise, but Joshua”
Aphrahat, *Dem.* 21.11 — “Joshua the son of Nun divided the inheritance unto his people; and Jesus our Redeemer has promised to give to the nations the land of life.”

label: Little fishes born in water
def: Believers as fish, born in water after the pattern of Christ the ICHTHUS, who live only by staying in the water.
christ: Christ is the ICHTHUS (Tertullian).
where: Tertullian, *Bapt.* 1 — “we, little fishes, after the example of our IChThUS Jesus Christ, are born in water”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 1 — “nor have we safety in any other way than by permanently abiding in water”
Augustine, *DDC* 3.32.45 — “the good fish and the bad are for the time mixed up in the one net.”

label: Melchizedek
def: A priest-king with no recorded beginning or end who brings out bread and wine to the victor.
christ: Melchizedek's bread and wine prefigure the sacrifice of Christ, the priest for ever after his order, who "offered that very same thing which Melchizedek had offered, that is, bread and wine, to wit, His body and blood" (Cyprian, *Ep.* 63.4 (ANF 62); so Augustine, *City of God* 16.22). Ambrose goes further and reads him as Christ Himself: "Do you recognize Who that is?" (*De Myst.* 8.46).
where: Cyprian, *Ep.* 63.4 (ANF 62) — “For who is more a priest of the most high God than our Lord Jesus Christ, who offered a sacrifice to God the Father, and offered that very same thing which Melchizedek had offered, that is, bread and wine, to wit, His body and blood?”
Augustine, *City of God* 16.22 — “For then first appeared the sacrifice which is now offered to God by Christians in the whole wide world”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 8.45 — “Melchisedech, who is introduced without father, without mother, having neither beginning of days, nor ending, but like the Son of God”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 8.46 — “Can a man be king of righteousness, when himself he can hardly be righteous?”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 4.3.10 — “Melchizedek. He, then, is the author of the sacraments.”

label: Moses as the one sent
def: A leader sent by God into the land of bondage to bring an oppressed people out through water.
christ: Moses figures Christ, who is sent from the Father into the world (Cyril, *Myst.* 1.3).
where: Cyril, *Myst.* 1.3 — “There we have Moses sent from God to Egypt; here, Christ, sent forth from His Father into the world”
Cyril, *Myst.* 1.3 — “here, that Christ might rescue those who are oppressed in the world under sin”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 5.1.3 — “Moses, that is to say, a prophet; the rod, that is the word of God.”

label: Moses' arms stretched out
def: While Joshua fights Amalek, Moses holds his hands out on the hilltop; Israel wins while they stay up and loses when they drop, so Aaron and Hur hold them up until sunset.
christ: The outstretched arms make the shape of the cross, and the battle is won by the one named Jesus (Joshua): "he who prevailed prevailed by the cross" (Justin, *Dial.* 90). Cyprian reads Amalek as the devil, overcome by Christ (*Test.* 2.16).
where: Justin, *Dial.* 90 — “For if he gave up any part of this sign, which was an imitation of the cross, the people were beaten”
Justin, *Dial.* 111 — “stretching out his hands, remained till evening on the hill, his hands being supported; and this reveals a type of no other thing than of the cross”
Barnabas, *Ep.* 12 — “the Spirit speaks to the heart of Moses, that he should make a figure of the cross, and of Him about to suffer thereon”
Tertullian, *Adv. Jud.* 10 — “the figure of the cross was also necessary, (that figure) through which Jesus was to win the victory?”
Cyprian, *Test.* 2.21 — “By this sign of the cross also Amalek was conquered by Jesus through Moses.”
Cyprian, *Test.* 2.16 — “Amalek was overcome by Jesus, that is, the devil was overcome by Christ.”

label: Mountain of refuge (Christ; the Church)
def: The mountain to flee to from judgment (Lot), read as Christ; elsewhere the Church.
christ: The mountain is Christ (Cyril, *Myst.* 1.8).
where: Cyril, *Myst.* 1.8 — “Was not he himself saved with his daughters, when he had gained the mountain”
Cyril, *Myst.* 1.8 — “escape to the mountain, to Jesus Christ, that stone hewn without hands, which has filled the world.”
Cyril, *Myst.* 3.7 — “now he calls the Church a mountain elsewhere also”

label: New beginning after the waters
def: The end state after passing through water: a new generation, regeneration, a second birth.
christ: The second creation comes "by means of His passion" (Irenaeus, *AH* 5.23.2).
where: Cyril, *Cat.* 17.10 — “the beginning of a new generation”
Cyril, *Cat.* 17.10 — “the true Noe, the Author of the second birth”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶5 — “Baptism, then, is a purification from sins, a remission of trespasses, a cause of renovation and regeneration.”
Irenaeus, *AH* 5.23.2 — “thus granting him a second creation by means of His passion, which is that [creation] out of death.”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 5 — “Thus man will be restored for God to His "likeness," who in days bygone had been conformed to "the image" of God”

label: Night to day
def: Movement from darkness or night to light or day, enacted in the descent and ascent of baptism.
christ: Christ is the pillar of light (Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 1.6.22).
where: Cyril, *Myst.* 2.4 — “in the descent, as in the night, ye saw nothing, but in ascending again ye were as in the day.”
Cyril, *Myst.* 1.4 — “the West is the region of sensible darkness”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶10 — “For as darkness is dispelled by light, and black disappears as whiteness is spread over it, so the old man also disappears”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 1.6.22 — “who scattered the shadows of unbelief, and poured the light of truth and spiritual grace on human hearts”

label: Olive branch, olive tree, oil
def: The olive (branch, tree, oil) as the sign of peace and of sharing in Christ's "fatness".
christ: Christ is the good olive tree (Cyril, *Myst.* 2.3). The exorcised oil means sharing in His fatness.
where: Tertullian, *Bapt.* 8 — “had returned with the olive-branch, a sign which even among the nations is the fore-token of peace”
Augustine, *DDC* 2.16.24 — “perpetual peace is indicated by the olive branch which the dove brought with it when it returned to the ark”
Cyril, *Myst.* 2.3 — “partakers of the good olive-tree, Jesus Christ.”
Cyril, *Myst.* 2.3 — “ye were cut off from the wild olive-tree, and grafted into the good one”
Cyril, *Cat.* 17.10 — “the dove returned to him towards evening with an olive branch”

label: One who comes down on the waters from above
def: A heavenly agent (Spirit, dove, angel, voice, fire) who comes down onto water or a sacrifice and makes it effective.
christ: Christ goes down into the water first and the Spirit follows, "that he might sanctify, and the Spirit also sanctify" (Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 1.5.18).
where: Tertullian, *Bapt.* 4 — “an underlying material substance should catch the quality of that which overhangs it”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 6 — “in the water, under (the witness of) the angel, we are cleansed, and prepared for the Holy Spirit.”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 5.26 — “When the Holy Spirit also speaks, Who came down in the likeness of a dove?”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 2.5.14 (on the dove) — “That unbelievers might be called to belief.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.14 — “the Holy Ghost cometh down on thee also, and a Father's voice sounds over thee from on high”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶5 — “that He might bring the Spirit from above, and exalt man to heaven”

label: Paradise / garden
def: The garden toward the east where man fell, which is reopened through the cross and baptism; read as the Church.
christ: Christ is buried in a garden and opens Paradise to the robber (Cyril, *Cat.* 13.19, 13.31).
where: Cyril, *Cat.* 13.19 — “In Paradise was the Fall, and in a Garden was our Salvation.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 13.31 — “thou by the Tree art brought into Paradise.”
Cyril, *Myst.* 1.9 — “there is opened to thee the paradise of God, which He planted towards the East, whence for his transgression our first father was banished”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶12 — “Thou didst banish us from Paradise, and didst recall us”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶12 — “Nor shall the flaming sword encircle Paradise around”
Irenaeus, *AH* 5.20.2 — “the Church has been planted as a garden (paradisus) in this world”
Irenaeus, *AH* 5.20.2 — “Eat ye from every Scripture of the Lord”

label: Pharaoh / the pursuing tyrant
def: An oppressor who pursues God's freed people to the water and is drowned there; read as the devil.
christ: Christ defeats the tyrant; the renunciation of Satan is said facing west (Cyril, *Myst.* 1.4).
where: Tertullian, *Bapt.* 9 — “the devil, their old tyrant, they leave quite behind, overwhelmed in the water.”
Cyril, *Myst.* 1.3 — “the tyrant was pursuing that ancient people even to the sea; and here the daring and shameless spirit, the author of evil”
Cyril, *Myst.* 1.3 — “The tyrant of old was drowned in the sea; and this present one disappears in the water of salvation.”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 3.12 — “wherein the Egyptian perished, the Hebrew escaped.”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶8 — “is choked with grief, and perishes, deeming the salvation of men to be his own misfortune.”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶8 — “Now let Laban be interpreted of the devil, and Jacob of Christ.”

label: Pillar of fire and cloud
def: The guiding pillar of light and the overshadowing cloud over the people in the sea.
christ: The pillar of light is Christ (Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 1.6.22). The cloud overshadows Mary at the Incarnation (Ambrose, *De Myst.* 3.13).
where: Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 1.6.22 — “What is the pillar of light but Christ the Lord”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 1.6.22 — “The pillar of cloud, on the other hand, is the Holy Spirit.”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 3.13 — “That kindly cloud overshadows those whom the Holy Spirit visits. At last it came upon the Virgin Mary”

label: Rahab's scarlet cord
def: The scarlet cord the harlot Rahab tied in her window at Jericho, so that she and everyone gathered in her house were spared when the city fell.
christ: The scarlet cord is the blood of Christ, which saves sinners from all the nations, like the blood of the passover on the doors; Rahab's house, outside which no one was safe, is the Church. By the cord it was shown "that redemption should flow through the blood of the Lord" (Clement of Rome, *1 Clem.* 12).
where: Clement of Rome, *1 Clem.* 12 — “she should hang forth from her house a scarlet thread. And thus they made it manifest that redemption should flow through the blood of the Lord”
Justin, *Dial.* 111 — “also manifested the symbol of the blood of Christ, by which those who were at one time harlots and unrighteous persons out of all nations are saved”
Irenaeus, *AH* 4.20.12 — “Rahab the harlot was preserved, when all was over [in ultimis], together with all her house, through faith of the scarlet sign”
Ambrose, *De Fide* 5.10.127 — “bound a scarlet thread in her window, and thus uplifted a sign of her faith and the banner of the Lord's Passion”
Augustine, *C. Faust.* 12.31 — “putting out of her window a scarlet line symbolical of blood, as confession is made with the mouth for the remission of sins”
Jerome, *Ep.* 52.3 — “it was a scarlet cord which the harlot Rahab (a type of the church) hung in her window to preserve her house in the destruction of Jericho”

label: Samson the Nazirite
def: The Nazirite judge whose birth an angel announces, who tears a lion and later finds honey in its carcass, and who dies pulling down the pillars of the Philistine temple, killing more enemies in his death than in his life.
christ: Jerome calls Samson "a type of the Saviour": he took a bride from the Gentiles, as Christ took the Church, and "slew more enemies in his death than he did in his life" (Jerome, *Adv. Jov.* 1.23). The lion he tore is death, which Christ destroyed, and the honey in its carcass is life for the nations (Ephraim, *Hymns on the Nativity* 8; Ambrose, *De Spir. S.* 2 prol. 6). A fragment attributed to Irenaeus reads his leaning on the two pillars as the people coming to recognise "the mystery of Christ" (*Fragments* 27).
where: Ephraim, *Hymns on the Nativity* 8 — “Samson the Nazarite shadowed forth a type of Thy working. He tore the lion, the image of death, whom Thou didst destroy”
Ephraim, *Hymns for the Epiphany* 2.25 — “In the honey of Samson--the nations tasted bitterness therein that destroyed them:--they had life in the Cross that redeemed them”

Jerome, *Adv. Jov.* 1.23 — “Samson continues to be a type of the Saviour because he loved a harlot from among the Gentiles, which harlot corresponds to the Church, and because he slew more enemies in his death than he did in his life”
Augustine, *C. Faust.* 12.32 — “when he killed the lion that met him as he went to get a wife among strangers, but He who, when going to call His Church from among the Gentiles”
Ambrose, *De Spir. S.* 2 prol. 6 — “The people of the Gentiles which believed had honey, the people which was before savage is now the people of Christ.”
Ambrose, *De Spir. S.* 2 prol. 8 — “Grace came forth from the offence, power from weakness, and life from death.”
Irenaeus (attributed), *Fragments* 27 — “The fact, then, of Samson leaning himself upon the pillars, [indicates] this, that the people, when instructed, recognized the mystery of Christ.”

label: Serpent
def: The deceiver in the garden whose head the woman's seed watches; but also, in a good sense, an image of wise self-renewal.
christ: Christ crushes the serpent's head (Irenaeus). In the bronze serpent the sign of death becomes the sign of the crucified (Cyril, *Cat.* 13.20).
where: Irenaeus, *AH* 5.21.1 — “was preached as keeping watch for the head of the serpent.”
Irenaeus, *AH* 5.19.1 — “the coming of the serpent is conquered by the harmlessness of the dove”
Cyril, *Myst.* 1.4 — “"I renounce thee,"--thou crafty and most subtle serpent.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.7 — “For every serpent creeps into a hole and casts its old slough, and having rubbed off the old skin, grows young again in body.”
Augustine, *DDC* 2.16.24 — “the serpent gets rid of its old skin by squeezing itself through a narrow hole, and thus acquires new strength”
Augustine, *DDC* 3.25.36 — “the serpent is used in a good sense, "Be wise as serpents;" and again, in a bad sense”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶5 — “drew along his serpent train, a disguise worthy of his own intent”

label: Serpent lifted on a pole
def: The bronze serpent fixed on a pole; those who looked at it lived.
christ: The crucified Son of God.
where: Cyril, *Cat.* 13.20 — “This was the figure which Moses completed by fixing the serpent to a cross”
Cyril, *Cat.* 13.20 — “Does then the brazen serpent save when crucified, and shall not the Son of God incarnate save when crucified also?”

label: Seven
def: A "legitimate" number put for universal time or completeness; Naaman's seven dips.
christ: Ambrose sets the seven dips "under the law" against baptism in the Trinity.
where: Augustine, *DDC* 3.35.51 — “"Seven times in the day do I praise Thee," means just the same as "His praise shall continually be in my mouth."”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 4.21 — “So that Syrian dipped himself seven times under the law, but you were baptized in the Name of the Trinity”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 3.16 — “he bade him dip himself seven times in the river Jordan.”

label: Spirit over the waters
def: The Spirit borne above the waters, who sanctifies whatever water He rests on.
christ: The same Spirit who hovered at creation "glided down on the Lord" at the Jordan (Tertullian, *Bapt.* 8).
where: Tertullian, *Bapt.* 4 — “the Spirit of God, who hovered over (the waters) from the beginning, would continue to linger over the waters of the baptized.”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 4 — “the Spirit immediately supervenes from the heavens, and rests over the waters, sanctifying them from Himself”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 8 — “Over the waters of baptism, recognising as it were His primeval seat, He reposes”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.5 — “before the whole six days' formation of the things that were made, the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the water.”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 3.9 — “He Who was moving upon the waters, was He not working upon the waters?”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 1.5.15 — “Water does not heal, unless the Spirit has descended and consecrated that water”

label: Stripping off and putting on
def: The old garment (old man, fig leaves, filthy rags) taken off at baptism; a white or costly garment put on.
christ: Christ is the garment put on (Cyril, *Myst.* 1.10; Gal 3:27). His nakedness on the cross strips the powers (Cyril, *Myst.* 2.2).
where: Cyril, *Myst.* 2.2 — “this was an image of putting off the old man with his deeds”
Cyril, *Myst.* 2.2 — “imitating Christ, who was stripped naked on the Cross”
Cyril, *Myst.* 2.2 — “ye bore the likeness of the first-formed Adam, who was naked in the garden, and was not ashamed.”
Cyril, *Myst.* 4.8 — “having put off thy old garments, and put on those which are spiritually white”
Cyril, *Myst.* 1.10 — “clothed in the garment of salvation, even Jesus Christ.”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶9 — “putting off our sins like some poor and patched garment, are clothed in the holy and most fair garment of regeneration.”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶12 — “Thou didst strip off the fig-tree leaves, an unseemly covering, and put upon us a costly garment”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 13 — “the clothing, in some sense, of the faith which before was bare”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.7 — “Put off the old man with his doings”

label: Swallowed and cast up
def: A prophet sleeps in a storm → is thrown into the sea → is swallowed by the monster → prays from Hades → is cast up on the third day → the nations repent.
christ: Jonah is the type of Christ's descent into Hades and His rising on the third day (Cyril). In Irenaeus, Jonah is also every person swallowed by the devil and given back.
where: Cyril, *Cat.* 14.17 — “Jonas was asleep in the ship, and snoring amidst the stormy sea; while Jesus also slept”
Cyril, *Cat.* 14.17 — “The one was cast into a whale's belly: but the other of His own accord went down thither, where the invisible whale of death is.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 14.20 — “I know, he says, that I am a type of Him, who is to be laid in the Sepulchre hewn out of the rock.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 14.20 — “though in the whale, he says that he is in Hades; for he was a type of Christ, who was to descend into Hades.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 4.12 — “Did Jonah come forth from the whale on the third day, and hath not Christ then risen from the earth on the third day?”
Irenaeus, *AH* 3.20.1 — “did God permit man to be swallowed up by the great whale, who was the author of transgression”
Irenaeus, *AH* 3.20.1 — “through the sign of Jonah”

label: The Bridegroom
def: Christ as the one who invites, washes and adorns the bride, and who also separates the unworthy guests.
christ: It is Christ.
where: Cyril, *Cat.* 3.2 — “For the Bridegroom invites all without distinction, because His grace is bounteous”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.2 — “but the same Bridegroom afterwards separates those who have come in to the figurative marriage.”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶12 — “the Adorner of the bride is Christ”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 7.37 — “But Christ, beholding His Church, for whom He Himself, as you find”

label: The Father's voice over the water
def: A voice from heaven over the waters naming the Son.
christ: Christ is the Son by nature. The baptized are sons "by adoption" (Cyril, *Cat.* 3.14).
where: Cyril, *Cat.* 3.14 — “a Father's voice sounds over thee from on high--not, "This is My Son," but, "This has now been made My son;"”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 5.26 — “the Father clearly calls from heaven in the Gospel narrative”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 1.5.19 — “Also God the Father spake from heaven. Thou hast the presence of the Trinity.”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶9 — “the inspired David, foretelling also the voice which the Father uttered from heaven upon the Son at His Baptism”

label: The Jordan
def: The river crossed into the land and used for washing and healing; where Christ was baptized; the source of all baptism.
christ: Christ sanctifies the Jordan by being baptized in it, and through it all waters (Cyril, *Cat.* 3.11; *Myst.* 3.1).
where: Cyril, *Cat.* 3.5 — “The water was the beginning of the world, and Jordan the beginning of the Gospel tidings”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.5 — “Elias is taken up, but not apart from water: for first he crosses the Jordan, then in a chariot mounts the heaven.”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶9 — “did not enter the land of promise until it had first been brought ... to the passage of the Jordan.”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶9 — “Jordan alone of rivers, receiving in itself the first-fruits of sanctification and benediction, conveyed in its channel to the whole world”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶9 — “the Jordan glorified by regenerating men and planting them in the Paradise of God”
Cyril, *Myst.* 3.1 — “He washed in the river Jordan, and having imparted of the fragrance of His Godhead to the waters, He came up from them”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 1.5.14 — “Then he went to Jordan, dipped, and arose whole.”

Cyril, *Cat.* 12.15 — “Christ came that He might be baptized, and might sanctify Baptism” … “the Lord took to Himself His body, that the sea might endure the sight, and Jordan receive Him without fear”

label: The bride (Church / soul)
def: The Church, or the baptized soul, prepared, washed and adorned for Christ the Bridegroom.
christ: The bride is Christ's body, the Church, and one speaker can be both, for "the head and the body--that is, Christ and His Church--are sometimes indicated to us under one person" (Augustine, *DDC* 3.31.44, on the first rule of Tyconius).
where: Cyril, *Cat.* 3.1 — “let the souls that are to be united to the spiritual Bridegroom make themselves ready.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.2 — “Begin at once to wash your robes in repentance, that when called to the bride-chamber ye may be found clean.”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶12 — “the Adorner of the bride is Christ”
Augustine, *DDC* 3.31.44 — “the head and the body--that is, Christ and His Church--are sometimes indicated to us under one person”
Augustine, *DDC* 2.6.7 — “the Church, when it is being praised under the figure of a beautiful woman”
Augustine, *DDC* 3.32.45 — “The Church declares itself to be at present both; and this because the good fish and the bad are for the time mixed up in the one net.”

label: The bush that burns unconsumed
def: The thorn bush on Horeb that Moses saw burning with fire and not burnt up, from which God called him by name and revealed Himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
christ: The one who spoke from the fire was the Word, the Son, before His incarnation (Justin, *1 Apol.* 63; Irenaeus, *AH* 4.5.2). The bush that burned without being consumed shows God coming into our flesh without destroying it: in the bush the Lord showed "that He would come to illuminate the thorns of our body" (Ambrose, *De Spir. S.* 1.14.165). An oration once credited to Methodius applies the bush also to the Virgin who bore Him.
where: Justin, *1 Apol.* 63 — “Jesus the Christ is the Son of God and His Apostle, being of old the Word, and appearing sometimes in the form of fire”
Irenaeus, *AH* 4.5.2 — “He who spake to Moses out of the bush, and declared Himself to be the God of the fathers, He is the God of the living.”
Clement of Alexandria, *Paed.* 2.8 — “the Word beheld at first in the bush, and afterwards taken up crowned by the thorn”
Ambrose, *De Spir. S.* 1.14.165 — “the bush was burning but was not consumed, because in that mystery the Lord was showing that He would come to illuminate the thorns of our body”
Ps.-Methodius, *Sim. et Ann.* 9 — “which beforehand shadowed forth thy figure endowed with divine majesty, bare God without being consumed”

label: The cross (the second tree)
def: The tree on which Christ, the second Adam, obeys; it answers the tree of the fall point for point.
christ: It is Christ's own cross. The outstretched hands gather two peoples under one head (Irenaeus, *AH* 5.17.4).
where: Irenaeus, *AH* 5.16.3 — “rectifying that disobedience which had occurred by reason of a tree, through that obedience which was [wrought out] upon the tree [of the cross].”
Irenaeus, *AH* 5.17.3 — “[so also] by means of a tree we may obtain the remission of our debt.”
Irenaeus, *AH* 5.17.4 — “there was one head in the middle, as there is but one God”
Irenaeus, *AH* 5.17.4 — “two hands, because there were two peoples scattered to the ends of the earth”
Cyril, *Cat.* 13.31 — “Adam by the Tree fell away; thou by the Tree art brought into Paradise.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 13.28 — “He stretched out His hands on the Cross, that He might embrace the ends of the world”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 2.7.23 — “Let the nail of Christ hold thee fast”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 8 (Jacob's crossed hands) — “by delineating Christ, they even portended the future benediction into Christ.”

label: The eighth day
def: The day after a full week of seven: the day a boy was circumcised, the day after the sabbath when the first sheaf was waved, and the number of souls saved in the ark.
christ: The eighth day is the first day after the sabbath, the day Christ rose, so it stands for the resurrection, the Lord's Day and the new creation. Circumcision on that day points to the true circumcision of the heart through "Him who rose from the dead on the first day after the Sabbath" (Justin, *Dial.* 41), and Barnabas calls it "a beginning of another world" (*Ep.* 15).
where: Justin, *Dial.* 41 — “The command of circumcision, again, bidding [them] always circumcise the children on the eighth day, was a type of the true circumcision”
Justin, *Dial.* 138 — “being eight in number, were a symbol of the eighth day, wherein Christ appeared when He rose from the dead”
Barnabas, *Ep.* 15 — “we keep the eighth day with joyfulness, the day also on which Jesus rose again from the dead.”
Cyprian, *Ep.* 64.4 (ANF 58) — “the eighth day, that is, the first day after the Sabbath, and the Lord's day, went before in the figure”
Augustine, *C. Faust.* 16.29 — “proved the circumcision of the eighth day to be also prophetical of Him.”
Augustine, *C. Faust.* 12.15 — “That Noah, counting his family, was the eighth; because the hope of our resurrection has appeared in Christ”

label: The flood shape
def: Corruption → waters purge the world → righteous carried in a wooden vessel → bird sent out → dove returns with peace → a new generation.
christ: Christ is the righteous Noah, the ark's wood is His cross, and the dove is the Spirit on Him at the Jordan. Tertullian warns that the world returned to sin after the flood, so the type does not fit in that respect.
where: Tertullian, *Bapt.* 8 — “after the waters of the deluge, by which the old iniquity was purged--after the baptism, so to say, of the world--a dove was the herald”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 3.10 — “You see the water, you see the wood [of the ark], you see the dove, and do you hesitate as to the mystery?”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 2.1.1 — “Is not the flood the same thing as baptism, whereby all sins are washed away, only the mind and grace of the righteous is revived”
Cyril, *Cat.* 17.10 — “by means of wood and of water there came salvation to themselves, and the beginning of a new generation”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.5 — “After the flood, a covenant was made with Noah”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 8 (the limit) — “the world returned unto sin; in which point baptism would ill be compared to the deluge.”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 1.6.23 — “if the figure of our baptism preceded, thou seest that the mysteries of the Christians are earlier than were those of the Jews.”

label: The iron raised by wood
def: Iron sinks in the water and is raised when wood is thrown in after it.
christ: The wood is the cross. In Irenaeus, the iron raised is the word of God that was lost.
where: Irenaeus, *AH* 5.17.4 — “he threw some wood into the water. Then, when he had done this, the iron part of the axe floated up”
Irenaeus, *AH* 5.17.4 — “For that the word of God is likened to an axe, John the Baptist declares”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 2.4.11 — “every man before baptism is weighed down like iron, and sinks”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 2.4.11 — “Dost thou see, therefore, how the weakness of all men is raised on the cross of Christ?”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 9.51 — “This, too, we clearly recognize as having happened contrary to nature, for iron is of heavier nature than water.”

label: The lamb and its blood
def: The lamb whose blood marks the doors so that the destroyer passes over.
christ: Christ is "the Lamb without blemish" (Cyril, *Myst.* 1.3): "the passover was Christ, who was afterwards sacrificed", and His blood delivers from death as the lamb's blood saved Israel in Egypt (Justin, *Dial.* 111).
where: Cyril, *Myst.* 1.3 — “there, the blood of a lamb was the spell against the destroyer; here, the blood of the Lamb without blemish Jesus Christ”
Justin, *Dial.* 40 — “The mystery, then, of the lamb which God enjoined to be sacrificed as the passover, was a type of Christ”
Justin, *Dial.* 40 — “that lamb which was commanded to be wholly roasted was a symbol of the suffering of the cross which Christ would undergo”
Justin, *Dial.* 111 — “For the passover was Christ, who was afterwards sacrificed”
Justin, *Dial.* 111 — “as the blood of the passover saved those who were in Egypt, so also the blood of Christ will deliver from death those who have believed”
Athanasius, *Festal Letter* 10 — “This is He Who in old time was sacrificed as a lamb, He being signified in the lamb”

label: The one who prepares the way
def: The servant who goes ahead, prepares by repentance and water, and points to the one greater who perfects.
christ: John prepares for Christ, who baptizes "in the Spirit and fire" (Tertullian, *Bapt.* 10).
where: Tertullian, *Bapt.* 6 — “In this case also a type has preceded; for thus was John beforehand the Lord's forerunner”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 10 — “it conveyed nothing celestial, but it fore-ministered to things celestial”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 10 — “he who "prepares" does not himself "perfect," but procures for another to perfect.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.6 — “Baptism is the end of the Old Testament, and beginning of the New.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.6 — “The end he was of the Prophets”

label: The red heifer
def: A spotless red heifer that had never borne a yoke was slain and burned whole outside the camp, and its ashes, mixed with water, cleansed those defiled by the dead.
christ: Christ, the spotless victim who suffered outside the gate: "The calf is Jesus" (Barnabas, *Ep.* 8). The ashes cleansed only the flesh; His blood, and the baptism it gives, cleanse the soul (Justin, Athanasius, Gregory Nazianzen).
where: Barnabas, *Ep.* 8 — “The calf is Jesus: the sinful men offering it are those who led Him to the slaughter.”
Theodoret, *Eranistes* III — “The image of the archetype is very distinctly exhibited by the lamb slain in Egypt, and by the red heifer burned without the camp”
Justin, *Dial.* 13 — “or by the ashes of an heifer, or by the offerings of fine flour, but by faith through the blood of Christ”
Athanasius, *Festal Letter* 14 — “Of old time, the blood of he-goats and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled upon those who were unclean, were fit only to purify the flesh”
Gregory Nazianzen, *Or.* 40.11 — “let us partake of the cleansing waters, more purifying than hyssop, purer than the legal blood, more sacred than the ashes of the heifer sprinkling the unclean”

label: The righteous one saved through the water
def: The one righteous man (with his household) kept alive through judgment to be the seed of a new world.
christ: Christ is "the true Noe" (Cyril, *Cat.* 17.10).
where: Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 2.1.1 — “What is the flood, but that in which the righteous is saved to be a seed-plot of righteousness, while sin dies?”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 2.1.1 — “he saved the righteous one alone with his offspring, but he bade the water rise even above the mountains.”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 3.10 — “God, willing to restore what was lacking, sent the flood and bade just Noah go up into the ark.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 17.10 — “the Holy Ghost also descended upon the true Noe, the Author of the second birth”

label: The rock that gives water
def: A rock struck in the desert that pours out water for a thirsty people.
christ: The Rock is Christ, "cloven by a stroke of the spear in His passion" (Cyprian, *Ep.* 63.8 (ANF 62)). The water from it is baptism (Tertullian, *Bapt.* 9; Cyprian), the cup (Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 5.1.3) and His blood (Ambrose, *De Myst.* 8.49a).
where: Tertullian, *Bapt.* 9 — “if Christ is "the Rock," without doubt we see baptism blest by the water in Christ.”
Cyprian, *Ep.* 63.8 (ANF 62) — “which is fulfilled in the Gospel, when Christ, who is the Rock, is cloven by a stroke of the spear in His passion”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 8.49a — “For them water flowed from the rock, for you Blood flowed from Christ”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 8.49b — “See now what happened in the case of the fathers was shadow”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 5.1.3 — “It was not an immovable Rock which followed the people. Drink thou also, that Christ may follow thee.”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 9.51 — “Moses touched the rock, and water flowed out of the rock.”

label: The shut east gate
def: The outer east gate of the sanctuary in Ezekiel's vision, kept shut for ever because the Lord God of Israel has entered by it, and opened to no one else.
christ: The gate is the Virgin Mary: the Lord came into the world through her and left her a virgin still, as He later came in to the apostles through shut doors. She is "the east gate, spoken of by the prophet Ezekiel, always shut and always shining" (Jerome, *Ep.* 48.21).
where: Jerome, *Ep.* 48.21 — “She is the east gate, spoken of by the prophet Ezekiel, always shut and always shining, and either concealing or revealing the Holy of Holies”
Rufinus, *Symb.* 9 — “That Gate of Virginity was closed; through it the Lord God of Israel entered; through it He came forth from the Virgin's womb into this world”
Ambrose (quoted in Cassian, *Incarn.* 7.25) — “As is said in Ezekiel: "And the gate was shut and not opened, because the Lord passed through it." A splendid Virginity, and wondrous fruitfulness!”
Ps.-Methodius, *Sim. et Ann.* 10 — “the gate through which God appears in the flesh”
John of Damascus, *Exp. fid.* 4.14 — “He who was born preserved her virginity intact, only passing through her and keeping her closed”

label: The sixth day (day of making and of dying)
def: The sixth day of creation, on which man was made and (Irenaeus argues) Adam died and Christ suffered.
christ: Christ "recapitulating in Himself this day" suffers on it, granting "a second creation" (Irenaeus, *AH* 5.23.2).
where: Irenaeus, *AH* 5.23.2 — “upon the day preceding the Sabbath, that is, the sixth day of the creation, on which day man was created”
Irenaeus, *AH* 5.23.2 — “the Lord suffered death, in obedience to His Father, upon that day on which Adam died while he disobeyed God.”

label: The stone (on the well; from the mountain)
def: A stone cut without hands, read as Christ born of a virgin; also the mountain refuge.
christ: It is Christ, born of a virgin without a human father (Gregory of Nyssa).
where: Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶8 — “For what is the stone that is laid but Christ Himself?”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶8 — “"A stone was cut out without hands," that is, Christ was born without a man.”
Cyril, *Myst.* 1.8 — “escape to the mountain, to Jesus Christ, that stone hewn without hands, which has filled the world.”

label: The troubled pool (Bethesda)
def: A pool where an angel from above stirs the water and the first to go down is healed.
christ: In *De Sacr.* the angel is Christ, "the Angel of Great Counsel". In *De Myst.* the paralytic waits for "the Lord Jesus, born of the Virgin" (4.24).
where: Tertullian, *Bapt.* 5 — “An angel, by his intervention, was wont to stir the pool at Bethsaida.”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 5 — “This figure of corporeal healing sang of a spiritual healing”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 4.22 — “They had a sign, you have faith; for them an angel descended, for you the Holy Spirit”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 4.23 — “that pool was as a type, that you might believe that the power of God descends upon this font.”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 2.2.3 — “Which signifies a figure of our Lord Jesus Christ who was to come.”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 2.2.4 — “Because he himself is the Angel of Great Counsel”

label: The veil torn in two
def: The woven curtain that hung before the holy of holies in the tabernacle and temple, shutting it off from all but the high priest once a year.
christ: The veil is Christ's flesh: when it was torn on the cross, the way into the holy place was opened and the hidden mysteries were laid bare. "Because His flesh, this veil, was dishonoured, therefore the typical veil of the temple was rent asunder" (Cyril, *Cat.* 13.32).
where: Cyril, *Cat.* 13.32 — “And because His flesh, this veil, was dishonoured, therefore the typical veil of the temple was rent asunder”
Chrysostom, *Hom. Heb.* 19 — “For this flesh first cut that way, by this He inaugurated it [the way] by which He walked.”
Leo, *Serm.* 68.3 — “the High Pontiff was entering the Holy of Holies, and to intercede with God the spotless Priest was passing in through the veil of His flesh”
Gregory Nazianzen, *Or.* 29.20 — “and the veil is rent, for the mysterious doors of Heaven are opened”
Augustine, *C. Faust.* 12.11 — “at the crucifixion of Christ, the veil was rent in twain, that by the passion of Christ hidden mysteries might be revealed to believers”

label: The washed-then-anointed priest and king
def: One washed in water and then anointed with oil to be priest or king; the name "Christ" comes from this.
christ: Christ is anointed with the Spirit, not with material oil (Cyril, *Myst.* 3.2). The baptized become "christs" by sharing in His anointing.
where: Tertullian, *Bapt.* 7 — “Whence Aaron is called "Christ," from the "chrism," which is "the unction;"”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 7 — “the unction runs carnally, (i.e. on the body,) but profits spiritually”
Cyril, *Myst.* 3.6 — “Aaron was called Christ or Anointed, evidently from the typical Chrism.”
Cyril, *Myst.* 3.6 — “in advancing Solomon to the kingdom, anointed him after he had bathed in Gihon”
Cyril, *Myst.* 3.1 — “Now ye have been made Christs, by receiving the antitype of the Holy Ghost”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.5 — “for Aaron first washed, then was made high-priest”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 6.30 — “we are all anointed with spiritual grace for a share in the kingdom of God and in the priesthood.”

label: The waters that prefigure baptism
def: The Fathers' master series of waters: creation → flood → Red Sea → Marah/rock → Jordan → Christ's baptism → font. Each one is a figure of baptism.
christ: Christ is at the centre of the series: He sanctifies the Jordan and every water after it, and water flows from His side.
where: Tertullian, *Bapt.* 9 — “How many, therefore, are the pleas of nature, how many the privileges of grace” ... “the figures, the preparations, the prayers, which have ordained the sanctity of water?”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 9 — “Never is Christ without water”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.5 — “The water was the beginning of the world, and Jordan the beginning of the Gospel tidings”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 2.3.9 — “thou hast a third kind when the fathers were baptized in the Red Sea; thou hast a fourth kind in the pool”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶7 — “the ancient Scripture everywhere prefigured the likeness of our regeneration”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 3.9 — “Consider, however, how ancient is the mystery prefigured even in the origin of the world itself.”

label: The well (meeting place of bride and water)
def: A well in the wilderness where life-saving water is given and where brides are found.
christ: Christ is the stone that lay on the well, "the spiritual stone, Christ, concealing in the deep and in mystery the laver of regeneration"; the one who rolls it away is Jacob, "Israel, who is mind seeing God", who gives living water to the flock of the Church (Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶8).
where: Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶8 — “an angel unexpectedly appears, and shows her a well of living water, and drawing thence, she saves Ishmael.”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶8 — “a marriage that was to produce the race of Christ had its beginning and its first covenant in water”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶8 — “for a type of all those impious men of later days who hindered the grace of Baptism”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶8 — “But Jacob alone rolls away the stone, and waters the flocks of his spouse.”

label: Thorns
def: The curse on the ground ("thorns and thistles"), which Christ takes on Himself as a crown.
christ: The crown of thorns cancels the curse on the ground.
where: Cyril, *Cat.* 13.18 — “For this cause Jesus assumes the thorns, that He may cancel the sentence”
Cyril, *Cat.* 13.18 — “for this cause also was He buried in the earth, that the earth which had been cursed might receive the blessing instead of a curse.”

label: Three / the third day
def: Three days (and three nights), three immersions, three pourings: the number of burial and resurrection.
christ: These are Christ's three days in the earth. The three immersions are also tied to the three Names (Gregory of Nyssa; Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 2.7.20–22).
where: Cyril, *Myst.* 2.4 — “descended three times into the water, and ascended again; here also hinting by a symbol at the three days burial of Christ.”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶5 — “by doing this thrice we represent for ourselves that grace of the Resurrection which was wrought in three days”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 2.7.20 — “that the triple confession might absolve the manifold fall of thy former life.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 4.12 — “Did Jonah come forth from the whale on the third day”
Augustine, *DDC* 3.35.50 — “we cannot make out the three days and three nights during which He foretold that He would be in the heart of the earth”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶9 — “the fire was kindled by water thrice poured upon it”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 6 — “wherever there are three, (that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, ) there is the Church”

label: Turning from west to east
def: West is the region of darkness and the devil; east is the region of light and Paradise; conversion is a turn from one to the other.
christ: To turn east is to turn to Christ (Ambrose).
where: Cyril, *Myst.* 1.4 — “Since the West is the region of sensible darkness, and he being darkness has his dominion also in darkness”
Cyril, *Myst.* 1.9 — “a symbol of this was thy turning from West to East, the place of light.”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 2.7 — “then you turned to the east; for he who renounces the devil turns to Christ, and beholds Him face to face.”

label: Twelve
def: A "legitimate" number standing for a whole; the twelve stones of the Jordan and the twelve apostles.
christ: The twelve are Christ's apostles, "the ministers of Baptism" (Gregory of Nyssa).
where: Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶9 — “Joshua also, who set up the twelve stones in the stream, was anticipating the coming of the twelve disciples, the ministers of Baptism.”
Augustine, *DDC* 3.35.51 — “our author calls those numbers legitimate which Holy Scripture more highly favors such as seven, or ten, or twelve”

label: Two goats of the Atonement
def: On the Day of Atonement two like goats were taken: one was slain as a sin offering, the other, laden with the people's sins, was driven out into the wilderness.
christ: Christ in both goats: the one driven out, cursed, spat on and bound with scarlet is His passion outside the city, the other His coming again, so that they are "declarative of the two appearances of Christ" (Justin, *Dial.* 40; so also Tertullian, *Adv. Marc.* 3.7). Theodoret reads them instead as His two natures, the manhood slain and the Godhead let go.
where: Barnabas, *Ep.* 7 — “why [do you behold] the one that is accursed crowned? Because they shall see Him then in that day having a scarlet robe about his body down to his feet”
Justin, *Dial.* 40 — “of which one was sent away as the scape [goat], and the other sacrificed, were similarly declarative of the two appearances of Christ”

Tertullian, *Adv. Marc.* 3.7 — “One of these goats was bound with scarlet, and driven by the people out of the camp into the wilderness … being thus marked with all the signs of the Lord's own passion; while the other … afforded proofs of His second appearance”

Tertullian, *Adv. Jud.* 14 — “marked with manifest tokens of Christ's passion; who, after being begirt with scarlet garment, and subjected to universal spitting, and afflicted with all contumelies, was crucified outside the city”
Theodoret, *Eranistes* III — “In these two goats there is an anticipative image of the two natures of the Saviour”

label: Type to antitype (shadow to body)
def: The time-axis from the earlier, bodily figure to the later, spiritual reality it foreshadows; the later is greater.
christ: The reality the figures point to is Christ and His sacraments (Irenaeus, *AH* 4.26.1).
where: Tertullian, *Bapt.* 5 — “according to the rule by which things carnal are always antecedent as figurative of things spiritual.”
Cyril, *Myst.* 1.3 — “Now turn from the old to the new, from the figure to the reality.”
Cyril, *Myst.* 2.5 — “our imitation was in a figure, and our salvation in reality.”
Cyril, *Myst.* 3.6 — “To them however these things happened in a figure, but to you not in a figure, but in truth”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 8.49b — “light is better than shadow, truth than a figure”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 2.1.2 — “And the mere figure helps us, since it is the herald of reality.”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 1.6.20 — “to them in a figure, but to us in reality.”
Origen, *DP* 4.1.11 (Lat.) — “the spiritual law itself (which has a shadow of good things to come)”
Irenaeus, *AH* 4.26.1 — “a treasure, hid indeed in a field, but brought to light by the cross of Christ”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶8 — “The thing is, I think, a dark saying, a shadow of what should come.”

label: Undoing by the same steps
def: The fall is undone by repeating its steps in reverse: virgin, tree, garden, evening, day, side. Each instrument of loss becomes an instrument of salvation.
christ: This is Irenaeus' "recapitulation": Christ sums up Adam in Himself and goes through each step again, the other way.
where: Irenaeus, *AH* 3.22.4 — “what is joined together could not otherwise be put asunder than by inversion of the process by which these bonds of union had arisen”
Irenaeus, *AH* 5.16.3 — “so was it also by these same that He brought in obedience”
Irenaeus, *AH* 5.19.1 — “virginal disobedience having been balanced in the opposite scale by virginal obedience.”
Irenaeus, *AH* 5.21.1 — “He has therefore, in His work of recapitulation, summed up all things, both waging war against our enemy”
Irenaeus, *AH* 5.23.2 — “by summing up in Himself the whole human race from the beginning to the end, He has also summed up its death.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 12.15 — “By the very same weapons, therefore, wherewith the Devil used to vanquish us, have we been saved.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 13.18 — “For this cause Jesus assumes the thorns, that He may cancel the sentence”
Cyril, *Cat.* 13.19 — “I am truly astonished at the truth of the types. In Paradise was the Fall, and in a Garden was our Salvation.”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 5.1.4 — “Because whence the guilt, thence the grace”

label: Waters of the beginning
def: The first waters of creation: unformed, life-bearing, and the "seat" of the Spirit, from which heaven and earth were drawn.
christ: The Fathers do not make the waters Christ. They are the Spirit's first seat, and every later water (Jordan, font) shares their "pristine privilege" once it is invoked over.
where: Tertullian, *Bapt.* 3 — “water is one of those things which, before all the furnishing of the world, were quiescent with God in a yet unshapen state.”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 3 — “Water was the first to produce that which had life, that it might be no wonder in baptism if waters know how to give life.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 3.5 — “the heavens are from the waters: the earth is the place of men, but the earth is from the waters”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 3.9 — “Consider, however, how ancient is the mystery prefigured even in the origin of the world itself.”

label: Waters that drown
def: Waters that destroy the wicked or the enemy while the righteous pass through or are carried over them.
christ: Christ goes down into these waters (at the Jordan and in death) and breaks the dragon there (Cyril, *Cat.* 3.11). In Him the drowning waters become a grave that is also a mother.
where: Tertullian, *Bapt.* 8 — “the waters of the deluge, by which the old iniquity was purged”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 9 — “it was water that extinguished the king himself, with his entire forces.”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 3.11 — “All wickedness is there buried.”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 2.1.1 — “in that flood all corruption of the flesh perished, only the family and pattern of the righteous survived.”
Cyril, *Myst.* 1.2 — “was all at once overwhelmed and engulphed in the Red Sea.”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 12 — “disquieted "in the sea," that is, in the world, "by the waves," that is, by persecutions and temptations”

label: Wood that saves
def: Any wood God uses to save (ark, rod, Marah wood, serpent-pole, Elisha's stick); all point to the cross.
christ: All of these woods point to the cross. Tertullian also makes the wood Christ Himself.
where: Cyril, *Cat.* 13.20 — “On each occasion life comes by means of wood. For in the time of Noe the preservation of life was by an ark of wood.”
Cyril, *Cat.* 13.20 — “is then Moses' rod mighty, and is the Cross of the Saviour powerless?”
Ambrose, *De Myst.* 3.11 — “The wood is that on which the Lord Jesus was fastened when He suffered for us.”
Ambrose, *De Sacr.* 2.4.11 — “Dost thou see, therefore, how the weakness of all men is raised on the cross of Christ?”
Irenaeus, *AH* 5.17.4 — “which we had negligently lost by means of a tree ... we should receive anew by the dispensation of a tree”
Tertullian, *Bapt.* 9 — “That tree was Christ”
Gregory of Nyssa, *Bapt. Chr.* ¶5 — “the wood of the Cross is of saving efficacy for all men”
Cyril, *Cat.* 17.10 — “He who by the wood of the Cross saves them who believe”
